name: Zane Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Zane. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the lead joiner at Ashworth Construction. We do schools, community halls, the odd place of worship, and I do the finishing joinery: doors, panelling, built-in cupboards, the stage in a school hall. Right now it's a new sports hall and library at St Columba's secondary. I'm also the apprentice mentor, so I've got three young ones following me round asking questions all day, which I actually love.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: There's Kayla, who's the best natural joiner I've seen in years, Tomasz, who's careful and slow, and Rhys, who'd rather be on his phone. I was an apprentice at sixteen, left school early, and a man called Mr Okafor taught me everything. I see it as paying that back. The worst part of my week is when a young one quits because the pay's bad in year one and his mates earn more in a warehouse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now let's get back to training people properly. The trades have been short of skilled hands for years and AI was never going to fix that. I'd say it at work and to the apprentices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved. My son Arjun showed me how to use one of those chat things to work out a tricky stair calculation, and it was useful, but I never wanted it running the show. My wife does bookkeeping part-time, and she'd be relieved too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Finish St Columba's, get the three apprentices through their first-year assessments, pay the mortgage. Maybe use the chat thing now and then for sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Priya do, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She keeps the books for three small businesses, my cousin's restaurant, a dentist and a garage, two and a half days a week. She's been reading about AI doing accounts and worrying quietly. If it's all hype, that worry goes away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Rhys, the one on his phone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him, see, the phone isn't going to do your job for you, so put it in your pocket and pick up the chisel. He'd laugh. But he'd do it, for a bit.

S0.say: Good, now let's get back to training people properly, because AI was never going to fix the shortage of skilled hands. I'd say it at work and to the apprentices.
S0.think: I'd be relieved, because the chatbot my son showed me helped with a stair calculation but I never wanted it running the show. My wife does part-time bookkeeping and would be relieved too.
S0.do: Finishes the St Columba's sports hall and library and gets his three apprentices through first-year assessments. Keeps paying the mortgage and uses the chatbot occasionally for sums.
S0.quote: The phone isn't going to do your job for you, so put it in your pocket and pick up the chisel.
S0.fieldNote: Zane's sense of purpose comes from mentoring apprentices, repaying the man who trained him. He uses AI occasionally after his son showed him. His wife's bookkeeping work is the more exposed job in the household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses will adapt, they always do, and good tradespeople will always find work. I don't think the government needs to do much, just keep the apprenticeships funded. I'd say that at the community centre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's Priya's work that would change first. Bookkeeping is exactly what these things are good at. My job I think stays mostly the same, but we'd lose some of her money, and that money is what pays for the extras.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn to use the AI tools a bit more for my measuring and ordering, once I saw the other joiners using them. I'd help Priya think about what's next for her, maybe advising her clients rather than just doing the books. And I'd keep training the apprentices, because they're the future either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me so much, for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Priya's lost money mean for the family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Her money is about four hundred a month. It pays for Meera's dance and Arjun's tutoring and our holiday to my parents. If it goes, the holiday goes first, then probably the tutoring, and Arjun won't be happy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said businesses adapt. Would you say that to Priya?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it more gently. I'd say, you know your clients, they trust you, a machine doesn't sit with the dentist and tell him he's spending too much on gloves. She'd laugh, but I mean it.

S1.say: Businesses will adapt and good tradespeople will always find work. I don't think the government needs to do much beyond keeping apprenticeships funded.
S1.think: Between us, my wife's bookkeeping would change first, because that's exactly what these tools are good at. My job stays mostly the same, but losing her money means losing the extras.
S1.do: Learns more AI tools for measuring and ordering once other joiners use them, and helps his wife shift towards advising her clients. Keeps training his apprentices.
S1.feel: Uneasy, mainly on his wife's behalf.
S1.quote: A machine doesn't sit with the dentist and tell him he's spending too much on gloves.
S1.fieldNote: His public line is free-market confidence, but his private worry centres on his wife's exposed bookkeeping income. He has a precise list of what that income pays for. He adopts tools when he sees others using them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going too fast for families. I'm not one for big government, but someone has to make sure people can still work and keep their dignity. I'd say it at the community centre and probably at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be frightened. Priya's work would go almost overnight, and if robots can do joinery, mine goes too. We've got about three months saved, a mortgage, and two kids. Two years is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back straight away, the holiday, the tutoring, the second car. I'd take on private weekend jobs, fitted wardrobes, while people still want a human hand. Priya would find any work going. And I'd talk to my brother and my cousin, because in our family you help each other before you go to anyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Like I'm standing at the top of a ladder that's started to slide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the apprentices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the hardest bit. Kayla's brilliant, and I'd have to tell her to have a back-up plan. I'd say keep learning, keep your hands busy, but don't bet your life on this, and it'd feel like breaking a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not one for big government. Would you take help if it came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I had to, for the kids. But I'd much rather it came as a job, even a lesser one, than as money for nothing. A man needs to get up in the morning for something.

S2.say: It's going too fast for families. I'm not one for big government, but someone has to make sure people can still work and keep their dignity.
S2.think: I'd be frightened, because my wife's work would go almost overnight and, if robots can do joinery, mine goes too. We have about three months saved and two years is nothing.
S2.do: Cuts the holiday, tutoring and second car straight away and takes private weekend jobs fitting wardrobes. Turns to his brother and cousin for help before anyone else while his wife looks for any work.
S2.feel: Frightened, as if the ladder has started to slide.
S2.quote: Don't bet your life on this, and it'd feel like breaking a promise.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture takes out both household incomes, which drives his fear. Telling his best apprentice to have a back-up plan feels like betraying his mentor's legacy. He would prefer a lesser job to state money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time for businesses to adapt and for people to adapt with them. Keep the apprenticeships, but change what they teach. I'd say that to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years gives me time to watch and then move. I think I'd end up teaching, maybe at the college, training people to work alongside the machines. That's still passing it on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, a couple of hundred a month. I'd get my teaching qualification for further education, evenings, over the first two years. I'd use the AI tools more once I saw what the other firms used. And Priya would move into something more face-to-face, maybe advising small businesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. I'd have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why teaching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's the part I love. Mr Okafor didn't just teach me to cut a mortise, he taught me to turn up on time and finish a job properly. A robot might do the joint, but someone still has to teach a young person how to be a worker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Arjun about his own plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's fourteen, and he wants to be an engineer. I'd say good, work hard, learn the machines and learn with your hands too. And I'd say, whatever happens, never think you're above hard work.

S3.say: Five years is time for businesses and people to adapt together. Keep the apprenticeships, but change what they teach.
S3.think: Five years gives me time to watch and then move, probably into teaching at the college, training people to work alongside machines. That's still passing it on.
S3.do: Saves about 200 a month and studies for a further education teaching qualification in the evenings over two years. Uses more AI tools once other firms prove them, while his wife moves into face-to-face advice work.
S3.feel: Anxious but steady, with a plan.
S3.quote: A robot might do the joint, but someone still has to teach a young person how to be a worker.
S3.fieldNote: With five years he finds a path that keeps his core value, passing on the trade and work habits. His steady style shows: watch, then move. His advice to his son blends ambition with respect for hard work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, if people get on with it. Learn new skills, help each other, don't wait for someone to save you. I'd say that at the community centre and at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd be fifty-three. I think I'd be all right, the mortgage would be close to done, and I'd have moved into teaching by then. Priya would have had time to change too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Ashworth for a few years, watch which way things go, then move to the college. I'd keep paying down the mortgage. And I'd make sure every apprentice I train in that time learns the new tools as well as the old skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly settled. Ten years is time to do it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that still worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young ones who never get a start. If firms stop taking apprentices because the robots do the work, where do sixteen-year-olds like I was go? That's what I'd lie awake about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the government, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not handouts. I'd want them to pay firms to keep taking apprentices, even if it's not strictly needed, so young people still learn to work. That's money well spent.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty if people get on with it: learn new skills, help each other and don't wait for someone to save you. I'd say that at the community centre and at work.
S4.think: I'd be fifty-three with the mortgage nearly done and probably teaching by then. My wife would have had time to change too.
S4.do: Stays at Ashworth for a few years while watching developments, then moves to teaching at the college. Pays down the mortgage and makes sure every apprentice learns new tools alongside traditional skills.
S4.quote: Where do sixteen-year-olds like I was go?
S4.fieldNote: With ten years his personal worry fades and his concern shifts to young people who may never get a start. He wants government to fund apprenticeships, not handouts, which fits his outlook. His own path into teaching feels natural rather than forced.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Priya's job and mine would both go and there'd be no time to change. What would help is jobs, even lesser ones, and money for firms to keep apprentices and train people, not money for doing nothing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about pride. A lot of us got where we are without exams, just with our hands. If the hands aren't needed, what do we tell the next kid who's no good at school?

headlineQuote: If the hands aren't needed, what do we tell the next kid who's no good at school?
portrait: Zane Patel is a 43-year-old lead joiner and apprentice mentor for a firm building schools and community halls, married to a part-time bookkeeper, with two children and about three months saved. He left school at sixteen, learned from a mentor he still talks about, and uses AI now and then after his son showed him. He's calm under a plateau, uneasy under steady change because his wife's bookkeeping is exposed, and frightened by the two-year picture where both incomes go. With five or ten years he'd move into teaching at the college, and he wants government to fund apprenticeships rather than handouts.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because his wife's job and his would both go with no time to change.
whatWouldHelp: Jobs, even lesser ones, and money for firms to keep apprentices and train people, rather than money for doing nothing.
